name: Laser lipolysis (SmartLipo)

lead: Laser lipolysis, best known by the SmartLipo brand, is a minimally invasive procedure in which a laser fiber is passed through a small incision to liquefy or heat fat, often followed by suction. People consider it for a slimmer jawline and neck with some skin tightening.

Laser energy at wavelengths such as 1064, 1320 or 1444 nm is absorbed by fat, disrupting fat cells and heating surrounding tissue, which authors say also stimulates collagen and skin contraction. Early reports describe less bleeding and more skin retraction than conventional liposuction; studies include a 30-subject Nd:YAG study and a retrospective analysis of 534 procedures with a diode laser.

paras: A clinician makes a small incision, passes the fiber under the skin, and may suction out the liquefied fat, usually under local anesthesia in the neck. Swelling settles over weeks and the contour sharpens as it does.

It is a surgical procedure with risks shared with liposuction, such as bleeding, infection, numbness and contour irregularities. Heating of tissue is a specific consideration, and thermal studies have examined temperature rise in treated tissue.

angle.text: Users consider laser-assisted fat removal for the neck and jawline for a leaner contour and some skin tightening. A laser fiber heats and disrupts fat under the skin, and the heat is said to tighten the skin as well. Early studies report fat reduction and tightening.

lead: Laser lipolysis, also called laser-assisted liposuction or by the SmartLipo brand, uses laser energy delivered through a thin fiber under the skin to disrupt fat cells, sometimes followed by suction removal. It is promoted for small areas, including the neck and jawline, and for tightening skin [1][2].

Early reports described a less traumatic technique than conventional liposuction with reduced bleeding and skin retraction [1]. Subsequent work includes a 30-subject Nd:YAG study [3], histologic and thermal studies [4][5], and a retrospective analysis of 534 procedures with a diode laser [6]. General liposuction carries recognized risks, which a Wikipedia overview summarizes [7].

paras: A thin laser fiber is introduced through a small incision into subcutaneous fat. The laser interacts with fat tissue, and the loosened fat may then be suctioned. Authors describe a less traumatic technique than conventional liposuction [1].

Histologic work on a pulsed Nd:YAG device (SmartLipo) examined its effects on excised human fat tissue [5]. Other studies compared wavelengths of 1064, 1320 and 2100 nm ex vivo [8], and examined tissue temperature rise during 1064/1320 nm treatment [4]. A mathematical modeling paper described laser lipolysis heat effects [9], and a study compared a 1,444 nm laser with a 1,064 nm laser, reporting a superior lipolytic effect for the former [10].

An early report described skin retraction in flaccid areas [1]. A 2006 study of 30 subjects with small fat areas used a 1,064 nm Nd:YAG laser, with MRI in some participants at baseline and 3 months [3]. A 2009 retrospective analysis of 534 procedures with a 980-nm diode laser has been published [6], and a 2016 paper described a combination approach to neck rejuvenation including laser lipolysis [2].

Liposuction in general has reported complications including infection, bleeding, numbness, seroma and contour irregularities, with rare serious events [7]. Thermal studies of laser lipolysis examine how much tissue heating occurs at different wavelengths and techniques [4].

Published human work is largely small prospective studies and retrospective series [1][3][6]. Several small trials of related devices are registered: a 1440 nm laser for the mandible and submandibular area (n=12, completed) [11], an LED device for non-invasive lipolysis (n=10, terminated) [12], a 1060 nm diode laser with other energy for non-invasive fat reduction (n=39, completed) [13], laser therapy with aerobic exercise (n=36, terminated) [14], and a 1064 nm diode laser/RF study (withdrawn) [15]. Results are not given in the available records.
